history.heading: Germanic tribes and the Holy Roman Empire
paragraphs: In antiquity Germanic tribes lived east of the Rhine; in 9 CE they defeated Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest, halting Roman expansion. After the division of Charlemagne's empire, the eastern Frankish kingdom developed into the Holy Roman Empire, founded with the coronation of Otto I in 962.

The empire was a loose patchwork of hundreds of states, cities and bishoprics. In 1517 Martin Luther launched the Protestant Reformation in Wittenberg, splitting Germany religiously. The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) devastated the region. Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, invented around 1450 in Mainz, transformed the world.

history.heading: Unification
paragraphs: Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. Prussia emerged as the leading German power, and after wars against Denmark, Austria and France, Otto von Bismarck unified Germany as the German Empire in 1871, with the Prussian king as emperor. Germany industrialised rapidly and became a great power.

history.heading: World wars and Nazism
paragraphs: Germany's defeat in the First World War led to the Weimar Republic, which suffered hyperinflation and the Great Depression. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party came to power in 1933 and established a totalitarian dictatorship.

Nazi Germany started the Second World War by invading Poland in 1939 and carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people and others. The war caused tens of millions of deaths, and Germany was defeated in 1945.

history.heading: Division and reunification
paragraphs: Germany was divided into the democratic Federal Republic (West Germany), which experienced an "economic miracle", and the communist German Democratic Republic (East Germany). The Berlin Wall, built in 1961, became a symbol of the Cold War.
The Wall fell on 9 November 1989, and Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. Germany became the leading economy of the European Union. Angela Merkel was chancellor from 2005 to 2021.

culture.heading: Thought and music
paragraphs: German is the official language and the most widely spoken native language in the EU. Germany is known as the "land of poets and thinkers": Goethe, Schiller, Kant, Hegel, Marx, Nietzsche and Thomas Mann are among its many influential figures.

Composers Bach, Beethoven, Brahms and Wagner shaped classical music. The Bauhaus school revolutionised design and architecture. Christianity is the largest religion, divided between Catholics and Protestants, with a sizeable Muslim minority and many non-religious people.

culture.heading: Traditions and food
paragraphs: Germany is famous for its beer culture, with the Reinheitsgebot (purity law) of 1516 and Munich's Oktoberfest, as well as bread, sausages, pretzels and regional dishes. Christmas markets originated in German-speaking lands.
Football is the most popular sport; Germany has won the men's World Cup four times. Germans are also known for their love of nature, hiking and cycling, and for strong environmental awareness.

politics.heading: Federal parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Germany is a federal parliamentary republic of 16 states (Länder). The chancellor leads the government and is elected by the Bundestag, the federal parliament. The Bundesrat represents the states. The president is head of state with mainly ceremonial duties.

Governments are typically coalitions. The main parties include the Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) and Social Democrats (SPD), as well as the Greens, the liberal FDP, and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which became the second-largest party in the 2025 election. After that election, the CDU/CSU and SPD formed a coalition government.

politics.heading: Germany in Europe and the world
paragraphs: Germany is a founding member of the European communities, a member of NATO and the G7, and the EU's most populous country. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it announced a turning point (Zeitenwende) in defence policy and became one of Ukraine's largest supporters, and in 2025 it loosened constitutional debt rules to fund defence and infrastructure.

economy.heading: Europe's largest economy
paragraphs: Germany has the largest economy in Europe and one of the largest in the world. It is a leading exporter of cars (Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes-Benz), machinery, chemicals (BASF), pharmaceuticals and electrical equipment (Siemens). Its strength lies partly in the Mittelstand, thousands of specialised medium-sized firms, and its dual vocational training system.
The currency is the euro, and Frankfurt hosts the European Central Bank.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: The German economy stagnated in 2023 and 2024, hit by high energy prices after the loss of cheap Russian gas, competition from China, especially in cars, an ageing workforce, bureaucracy and underinvestment in infrastructure and digitalisation. The Energiewende (energy transition) has expanded renewables while phasing out nuclear power, which ended in 2023.
